# Results — Study 30 (House-Edge) on the real S&P 500

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily S&P 500 total-return proxy (`^GSPC`,
auto-adjusted) and the 13-week T-bill (`^IRX`) as the financing rate, 1990–2026. The strategy is a
vol-targeted contrarian dip-buyer (RSI(2) entries, `target_vol/realised_vol` sizing, 200-day trend gate)
run under two honest account types — **margin** (borrow only the slice above 100% at bill + markup, idle
cash earns the bill) and **futures/CFD** (the whole notional carries bill + markup, capital stays in
bills). The two coincide exactly at a zero markup; what separates them is where the broker's markup lands.
Sharpe is quoted on returns **in excess of the bill** for every row, buy-and-hold included, so the financed
book and the index are compared on the same footing. The offline core proves the machinery on a synthetic
GARCH-with-bear-regimes index; this is the measurement on the market. As-of **2026-06-10**; match the
fingerprint below.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `REAL` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · Free leverage? `Busted`

The risk management is real and the "beat the market" promise is a mirage — and the exact line where the
dream dies is the **retail financing markup**, not financing itself. The vol-targeted, trend-gated book
**more than halves the worst drawdown** — **−24.7%** versus buy-and-hold's **−55.7%** — and *doubles* the
Calmar (0.38 vs 0.19). Funded at the fair bill rate (a zero markup — roughly what index futures roll near),
it almost matches the index: CAGR **10.1%** vs **10.6%**, at a slightly *better* excess Sharpe (**0.54** vs
**0.50**). There is no return edge even there — but there is no catastrophe either. The catastrophe is
retail funding: at the **1.5–3%** markup a CFD actually charges — on the **whole notional**, not the
borrowed slice — the book earns **7.4%** vs the index's **10.6%** and the excess Sharpe sinks to **0.38**.
What you can genuinely buy here is cheap drawdown insurance (a margin account pays ~**0.7 pts/yr** for a
31-point drawdown cut); what you cannot buy, at any markup, is out-earning the index you're levering.

## The house edge — where the markup lands

Same exposure path (average **0.97×**), same 2.5% markup, two account types: the margin account pays it
only on the borrowed slice (**0.66 pts/yr**), the CFD pays it on the **full notional** (**2.65 pts/yr** —
≈ avg exposure × markup). The difference — **~2 pts/yr charged on money you never borrowed** — is the
broker's house edge, and it is what separates "roughly matches the index with half the drawdown" from
"gives back a third of the market's return".

## Where the dream dies — the markup sweep, both account types

Edge vs the total-return hold (CAGR) and excess Sharpe, as the broker markup over the T-bill rises:

| markup over T-bill | margin CAGR | margin Sharpe | margin edge | CFD CAGR | CFD Sharpe | CFD edge |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.0% | 10.1% | 0.54 | −0.5% | 10.1% | 0.54 | −0.5% |
| 1.0% | 9.8% | 0.52 | −0.8% | 9.0% | 0.47 | −1.6% |
| 1.5% | 9.7% | 0.52 | −0.9% | 8.5% | 0.44 | −2.1% |
| 2.5% | 9.4% | 0.50 | −1.2% | 7.4% | 0.38 | −3.2% |
| 5.0% | 8.7% | 0.46 | −1.8% | 4.8% | 0.21 | −5.7% |

Two readings, both honest. First: the CAGR edge is negative in every row — the levered book never
*out-earns* the index, so "lever a good signal and beat the market" fails even at frictionless funding
(volatility drag and time spent gated out see to that). Second: at a zero markup the shortfall is a
rounding error (**−0.5 pts** on 10.6, with a better Sharpe and double the Calmar) — the *strategy* is fine;
it's the **retail markup** that turns a near-tie into a 2–3 pt/yr structural loss, and on a CFD it does so
on your entire position.

## The part that is real — drawdown protection

| | strategy (margin @ 2.5%) | buy & hold |
|---|---|---|
| max-drawdown | **−24.7%** | −55.7% |
| Calmar | **0.38** | 0.19 |

The worst drawdown falls by **30.9 points** — better than halved — and per unit of drawdown survived the
strategy now pays *twice* what the index does (Calmar 0.38 vs 0.19). Genuine, robust risk control, and in a
margin account it costs about **0.7 pts/yr** of CAGR plus the **0.5-pt** structural shortfall: cheap
insurance, honestly priced. Just don't let anyone sell it to you as a market-beater, and don't fund it
through a CFD. Signal `REAL`, Tradability `MIRAGE`, free leverage? `Busted`.
